fields.privacy_banner_text: How Caspian & Sun Food Trading LLC collects, uses and protects your information.
fields.privacy_lead: Your privacy matters to us. This policy explains what personal information we collect when you visit our website or contact us, how we use it, and the choices you have.

privacy_sections.title: Who we are
privacy_sections.content:
This website is operated by Caspian & Sun Food Trading LLC (“Caspian”, “we”, “us”), a food trading company supplying seafood, meat and poultry products to wholesale, hospitality and retail customers worldwide.

For the purposes of this policy, we are the party responsible for deciding how and why your personal information is used.

privacy_sections.title: Information we collect
privacy_sections.content:
We collect only the information we need to respond to you and to run our website:

  • Information you give us — such as your name, email address, phone number, company name and the content of your message when you use our contact form, enquire about a product, or write to us.
  • Enquiry details — the product, size or quantity you ask about.
  • Technical information — such as your IP address, browser type, device, pages visited and time spent, collected automatically through cookies and similar technologies.

privacy_sections.title: How we use your information
privacy_sections.content:
We use your information to:

  • respond to enquiries and prepare quotations;
  • arrange, deliver and support orders and shipments;
  • send service messages relating to your enquiry or account;
  • improve our website, products and customer experience;
  • meet legal, tax, customs and food-safety obligations.

We do not sell or rent your personal information to anyone.

privacy_sections.title: Sharing your information
privacy_sections.content:
We share information only where it is necessary to serve you, and only with:

  • logistics, cold-chain and customs partners who help deliver your order;
  • service providers who host our website or provide email, analytics or IT support, under confidentiality obligations;
  • authorities or advisers when we are required to by law or need to protect our legal rights.

privacy_sections.title: Cookies and analytics
privacy_sections.content: Our website uses cookies — small files stored on your device — to keep the site working, remember preferences and understand how visitors use it. You can block or delete cookies in your browser settings; some parts of the site may then work less smoothly.

privacy_sections.title: How long we keep information
privacy_sections.content: We keep personal information only for as long as needed for the purposes above, including to satisfy legal, accounting and food-traceability requirements. When it is no longer needed we delete or anonymise it.

privacy_sections.title: Keeping your information secure
privacy_sections.content: We use reasonable technical and organisational measures to protect personal information from loss, misuse and unauthorised access. No method of transmission over the internet is completely secure, so we cannot guarantee absolute security.

privacy_sections.title: International transfers
privacy_sections.content: We supply customers in many countries, so your information may be processed in countries other than your own, including where we or our service providers operate. Where this happens we take steps to keep it protected in line with this policy.

privacy_sections.title: Your rights
privacy_sections.content:
Depending on where you live, you may have the right to:

  • ask for a copy of the personal information we hold about you;
  • ask us to correct information that is inaccurate;
  • ask us to delete your information or restrict how we use it;
  • object to certain uses, including direct marketing.

To exercise any of these rights, contact us using the details below. We may need to verify your identity before acting on a request.

privacy_sections.title: Third-party links
privacy_sections.content: Our website may link to other websites, including social media. We are not responsible for the content or privacy practices of those sites, and encourage you to read their policies.

privacy_sections.title: Children
privacy_sections.content: Our website and services are intended for businesses and adults. We do not knowingly collect personal information from anyone under 18.

privacy_sections.title: Changes to this policy
privacy_sections.content: We may update this policy from time to time. The latest version will always be on this page with a revised “last updated” date. Continued use of the website after a change means you accept the updated policy.

privacy_sections.title: Contact us
privacy_sections.content: Questions about this policy or your information? We are happy to help.

posts.title: The Rising Demand for Premium Seafood in Global Markets
posts.excerpt: Hotels, restaurants and retailers worldwide are placing greater value on quality, provenance and consistency in seafood.

fields.article_body:
Seafood is one of the most widely traded food commodities in the world, and demand for premium products continues to grow as consumers and hospitality operators look for provenance, freshness and consistency. Industry analysis from organisations such as the FAO points to rising global consumption of aquatic foods, driven by population growth, rising incomes and a steady shift towards protein-rich diets.

Within that growth, the premium segment is distinct. Luxury hotels, fine-dining restaurants and upscale retailers are not simply buying more seafood; they are asking for specific species, specific origins and specific grades. King crab from cold northern waters, Canadian lobster, Hokkaido scallops and caviar each carry a story that chefs and guests recognise and value.

For importers and distributors, this places a premium on sourcing relationships. Reliable access to trusted producers, clear documentation and dependable cold-chain logistics are what allow a product to reach the kitchen in the condition the chef expects. Markets in the Middle East, where hospitality is a major driver of food demand, are a clear example.

At Caspian & Sun Food Trading, we see the same pattern across our customers: quality and reliability come first, and price is judged against both. That is why we work directly with producers in the regions best known for each product.

posts.title: Understanding the Importance of Reliable Food Sourcing
posts.excerpt: Why consistent supply, verified suppliers and transparent processes matter more than ever to foodservice businesses.

fields.article_body:
For a hotel or restaurant group, a missing ingredient is not a minor inconvenience. It can mean a changed menu, disappointed guests and lost revenue. Reliable sourcing is therefore less about finding a product once and more about securing it repeatedly, to the same specification, season after season.

A dependable sourcing partner begins with supplier selection. Product quality, certifications, production standards and track record are the criteria that separate a producer who can supply occasionally from one who can supply consistently. Food safety systems and traceability are equally important, particularly for products that cross several borders before reaching the customer.

Sourcing also depends on logistics. Temperature control, correct packing formats and accurate documentation protect product quality and avoid delays at the border. Working with international standards such as those developed under Codex Alimentarius gives buyers and sellers a common reference point.

The result of a well-managed sourcing relationship is predictability: stable quality, dependable delivery and pricing that can be planned around. It is the foundation on which long-term partnerships between producers, traders and customers are built.

FAO, Food safety and quality
WTO, Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures

posts.title: From Origin to Table: What Defines Premium Seafood?
posts.excerpt: Species, origin, handling and grading all shape the quality of premium seafood long before it reaches the plate.

fields.article_body:
Premium seafood is defined by a combination of factors rather than a single label. Species and origin matter, because different waters produce different textures and flavours. Harvest method and timing matter, because they affect freshness and yield. Handling and processing matter, because even an excellent catch can lose quality if it is not chilled or frozen correctly.

Grading and sizing are the next layer. Scallops are sold by size grade, shrimp by count per kilogram, and crab by cluster or leg size. These specifications allow chefs to plan portions and costs with confidence, and they allow buyers to compare like with like across suppliers.

Cold-chain integrity is what carries quality from origin to table. Products such as king crab legs, lobster and scallops are typically frozen at source to lock in freshness, then transported at controlled temperatures and thawed only when needed in the kitchen.

Finally, premium seafood is backed by documentation: certificates of origin, health certificates and traceability records. For hospitality businesses, this paperwork is as important as the product itself, because it demonstrates that what is on the plate is what was promised.

posts.excerpt: From provenance storytelling to specialty species, the trends influencing how hotels, restaurants and caterers buy seafood.

fields.article_body:
The HORECA sector, covering hotels, restaurants and catering, is one of the most influential buyers of seafood worldwide. Its purchasing choices reflect wider changes in how people dine, and several trends are shaping what reaches the menu.

Provenance is one. Guests increasingly want to know where their food comes from, and menus now name the origin of a scallop, a shrimp or a cut of fish. Specialty species are another: products such as carabinero shrimp, Hokkaido scallops and black cod have moved from niche ingredients to recognised menu highlights.

Consistency and portion control are a third. Kitchens that serve many covers need products in reliable sizes and formats, which is why grading and packing specifications matter so much in foodservice supply.

Finally, responsible sourcing and food safety continue to rise up the agenda. Buyers expect documented standards and dependable suppliers, and they increasingly favour partners who can provide both quality and transparency across the supply chain.

posts.title: How International Food Sourcing Supports Premium Hospitality
posts.excerpt: Why luxury hospitality relies on a global network of producers to deliver the products guests expect.

fields.article_body:
Premium hospitality is built on experience, and the ingredients on the plate are a large part of that experience. No single country produces every product a luxury kitchen requires, which is why international sourcing is central to high-end foodservice.

The best-known producers of a product are often far from the market that wants it: lamb and beef from Australia, scallops from Japan, lobster from Canada, poultry and foie gras from France and Hungary, carabinero shrimp from Spain. Connecting those producers with hotels and restaurants in the Middle East requires experience in export documentation, cold-chain logistics and quality control.

An international sourcing partner takes on that complexity on behalf of the customer. It evaluates suppliers, manages specifications, coordinates shipping and handles compliance, so the chef can focus on the menu rather than the supply chain.

When a specific product is not in a trader's portfolio, a strong sourcing network can also locate it. That flexibility, responding to a customer's exact requirement, is what distinguishes a supply partner from a simple supplier.

posts.title: Inside the World of Premium Meat, Poultry and Seafood
posts.excerpt: A look at what sets premium proteins apart, and how origin shapes flavour, texture and value.

fields.article_body:
Premium proteins share a common thread: origin and production method shape the final product. Australian Black Angus is valued for its marbling and tenderness, Argentine beef for its full-bodied flavour, and American Angus for its range of grades and cuts. Each serves a different kind of kitchen and menu.

Poultry follows the same logic. French yellow chicken is known for its golden skin and delicate flavour, corn-fed baby chicken from Spain for its compact size and tenderness, and duck and foie gras from France and Hungary for their place in classical European cuisine.

Seafood adds a further dimension. Cold-water species such as king crab and lobster, and delicate products such as scallops and caviar, depend on careful handling from harvest through to delivery.

Across all three categories, a professional buyer looks at the same fundamentals: specification, consistency, documentation and dependable supply. Sourcing from recognised producing regions, through an experienced partner, is the most reliable way to secure all four.

posts.title: Understanding Food Supply Chains: From Producer to Market
posts.excerpt: How a premium food product travels from producer to customer, and where quality is won or lost.

fields.article_body:
A food supply chain is a series of connected steps: production or harvest, processing, packing, storage, transport, customs clearance and final delivery. Each step is an opportunity to protect quality and each is also a point where it can be lost.

At the start of the chain, producer selection and quality standards set the ceiling for everything that follows. Processing and packing then determine how well a product tolerates long-distance transport, particularly for frozen and chilled goods.

Transport and storage depend on an unbroken cold chain and on accurate paperwork. Certificates, permits and labelling must match the requirements of the destination market, or shipments may be delayed or rejected.

An effective trading partner coordinates these steps end to end. By managing sourcing, logistics and compliance together, it shortens lead times, reduces risk and gives customers a single point of accountability from producer to market.
